newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-Heineken 96 profit flat, sees growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Heineken 96 profit flat, sees growth.

text.p: Heineken, Europe's biggest brewer, reported a slight dip in 1996 profits on Friday but its shares rose sharply as the market welcomed prospects for profit growth in 1997 and beyond.
Net profits totalled 655 million guilders ($342 million), down slightly from 664 million in 1995, with net profit per share of 13.06 guilders versus 13.24.
Analysts had expected net profit of between 630 and 660 million guilders and the shares staged a rally after suffering a hangover earlier in the week from rival Grolsch's gloomy profits and outlook.
Heineken shares jumped 15.50 guilders, or around five percent, in early trade before easing back to close 8.50 guilders higher at 338.
The brewer said it foresaw profit growth in 1997, although it added it was too early to quantify this.

"The changes in the world are a huge challenge to us...We closely watch the delicate balance between short- and long-term profit growth," chief executive officer Karel Vuursteen told a press conference.
"I think their comments on 1997 are not bad. Usually, they don't give a forecast for the year at such an early stage but stick to long-term prospects," said analyst Hans Pluijgers of Kempen & Co.

Operating profit was little changed at around 1.01 billion guilders, while turnover, boosted by recent acquisitions, grew by 20 percent to 12.19 billion guilders from 10.14 billion. The dividend was maintained at 3.50 guilders per share.

Vuursteen said the European beer market -- still seen as Heineken's main cash generator in the coming years -- would continue to stagnate but added the premium and speciality segments would rise further.
"In all modesty, I would like to say that with our brand portfolio, we are better positioned than our competitors and therefore don't consider ourselves vulnerable," he said.
Analysts said Heineken's global reach also gave it a good base for profit expansion.

"Everybody can brew beer. What counts is marketing and distribution. Heineken is the world's most international brewer when looked at by geographical spread. It's always one step ahead when moving into growth markets," said Cees Haasnoot at Effectenbank Stroeve.

While the North American beer market showed signs of saturation, growth segments could be found at the upper end of the market and Heineken would extend the Amstel brand this year on the east coast, Vuursteen said.
"In spite of the the stable market, we expect the U.S. will also in the future contribute to a further increase in profits," he said.
Heineken said earlier consumption in Asia and Latin America would show continued, albeit decreasing, growth.
Vuursteen said the situation of the emerging markets varied, with activities in some, such as Vietnam and Thailand, now profitable, while China was one of the world's least profitable.
He said Heineken would ensure long-term growth by investing in brands, technology and acquisitions, aiming for increased productivity and cost effectiveness.
Heineken said its exports were a particularly positive feature, growing by 10 percent in 1996.
It said the world beer market grew by 1.4 percent in 1996, while total sales of beer brewed under its supervision rose by 10 percent to 70.7 million hectolitres.
Sales of the Heineken branded beer rose 4.6 percent to 17.9 million hectolitres.
The Amstel brand maintained its sales volume of 6.9 million hectolitres in a declining segment market, while the Murphy's stout brand showed significant growth, the company said.

"The confidence of the company has increased in the past six months," said Gerard Rijk of ING Barings. "There are many positive factors. We had Heineken as a buy, that will stay and it should now start to outperform."
Beer consumption was down in most parts of Europe in 1996, hit by cooler summer weather and weaker economies, but these lower sales were offset by gains in volumes in America and Asia.
"You have to differentiate between incidental and structural factors... A bad summer does not say anything about the company's fundamentals," Haasnoot said.
